analysis: The closest option develops calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, probability and signals and applies these methods to motion, learning and decisions. Networks and operating systems supply computing context. Discrete Mathematics includes introductory proof, but Groningen requires deeper proof-based analysis and topology, a longer differential-equations sequence, dedicated systems theory and assessed projects.

The Earth option uses environmental modelling, geological field measurements, soils and aquifers, geochemical modelling, recycling experiments and renewable system assessment. Energy & Sustainability replaces Robotics, supplying preparation in energy demand, storage and generation before Renewable System Design. The difference from the closest route is a natural and technological systems application sequence.

The bioscience option combines epidemiology, molecular and cellular biology, anatomy, neuroscience, physiology, pathology and laboratory work with regression, imaging, numerical computation and signals. The courses support quantitative study of living systems without implying a sustained mathematical biology specialization. Technical image analysis remains distinct from clinical imaging instrumentation.

The two named stable directions overlap strongly in their UCR feasibility basis, so the closest option integrates them. The three feasible schedules are distinct, and no separate option is needed for a transient physics or biology example. Alignment was tightened to actual concepts and tasks. Advanced Algorithms and general academic formation remain useful UCR courses with no direct comparator row.

alignment.rationale: Both use programming to solve problems. Groningen builds directly on calculus and linear algebra in scientific programming.
Both use logic, sets and proof. Groningen continues this foundation into proof-based analysis.
Both introduce differentiation and integration. UCR also uses complex numbers and differential equations in a dynamic modelling project.
Both address optimisation; UCR focuses on search and constraint-satisfaction methods for AI rather than a full applied-mathematics optimisation course.
Both directly study systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces; Groningen continues to a second dedicated linear-algebra course.
Both study numerical integration, interpolation and equation solving. UCR tests accuracy and stability using Mathematica, while Groningen uses Python.
Both use differential equations to analyse linear systems. UCR emphasizes signals, transforms and feedback. Groningen continues into advanced systems theory.
Both establish probability concepts and distributions; UCR combines probability with statistical inference and simulation.
Both develop statistical models; UCR teaches regression, classification and machine-learning methods rather than Groningen's dedicated Statistical Modelling elective.
Both extend calculus to several variables. UCR also introduces complex-valued functions and differential equations.
